blocks.text: Model parallelism splits the model itself across multiple devices, rather than splitting the training data the way data parallelism, covered in the previous topic, does, solving a fundamentally different problem, a model simply too large to fit on any single device.
This topic introduces the general model parallelism idea, setting up the more specific tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism techniques covered in the next two topics of this module.
1. What Model Parallelism Means

blocks.alt: A model too large for one device gets split across devices instead

blocks.text: When a model genuine size exceeds what a single device can hold, model parallelism divides the model itself, its layers or its individual weight matrices, across multiple devices, so each device holds only a portion of the full model rather than a complete copy.
2. Splitting the Model Itself Across Devices

blocks.alt: Device one holds early layers, device two holds middle layers, device three holds later layers

blocks.text: A simple form of model parallelism assigns different layers of a deep network to different devices, device one processes the earliest layers, device two continues with the next set of layers, and so on, with data flowing sequentially between devices as it moves through the model.
3. Why Model Parallelism Solves a Different Problem Than Data Parallelism

blocks.alt: Data parallelism splits the batch while model parallelism splits the model

blocks.text: Data parallelism, covered in the previous topic, assumes the model already fits on one device and simply wants to process more data faster, while model parallelism specifically addresses the case where the model itself does not fit, a fundamentally different constraint requiring a fundamentally different solution.

blocks.text: 4. A Simple Layer Split Example

blocks.alt: Layer ten output gets sent to the next device as layer eleven input

blocks.text: As data moves through a model split this way, the output from the last layer on one device needs to be transferred to the next device before computation can continue there, introducing a communication step between devices that has to happen for every forward and backward pass.

code.content:
# A simplified layer-split model parallelism pattern
def forward(input_data):
    output_device1 = device1_layers(input_data)
    output_device1_transferred = transfer_to_device(output_device1, target="device2")
    output_device2 = device2_layers(output_device1_transferred)
    return output_device2

blocks.text: 5. Model Parallelism's Underutilization Risk

blocks.alt: Device one works now while device two sits idle, waiting

blocks.text: A naive layer split model parallelism setup can leave devices idle much of the time, while device one is actively computing its layers, device two has nothing to do yet since it needs device one output first, an inefficiency that pipeline parallelism, covered in the next topic, is specifically designed to address.

blocks.title: This idle time problem motivates the next topic in this module
blocks.content: The pipeline bubble problem covered in the Pipeline Parallelism topic is exactly this underutilization issue, and understanding it here makes that upcoming topic solution far more meaningful.

blocks.text: 6. Model Parallelism vs Data Parallelism

blocks.alt: Model parallelism is compared against data parallelism

blocks.text: Model parallelism trades some device utilization efficiency for the ability to train a model that data parallelism alone could never accommodate, since data parallelism strictly requires a full model copy per device, a requirement model parallelism specifically exists to remove.
7. Combining Model and Data Parallelism

blocks.alt: Model parallelism fitting a large model combines with data parallelism processing more data

blocks.text: Real large scale training setups often combine both techniques together, model parallelism splits the model across a group of devices so it fits at all, while data parallelism replicates that entire split model group to process multiple batches simultaneously, getting the benefits of both approaches at once.
8. When Model Parallelism Is Necessary

Model parallelism becomes necessary specifically when a model, even after applying the memory saving techniques covered in earlier modules, quantization, PEFT, gradient checkpointing, still does not fit on the largest single device available, a scenario most common with the very largest models covered throughout this course.
9. Model Parallelism's Complexity Cost

Compared to the relatively straightforward data parallelism covered in the previous topic, model parallelism introduces meaningfully more implementation complexity, coordinating data transfer between devices correctly and managing device utilization, which is why frameworks that handle this complexity automatically, covered later in the Fine-Tuning Frameworks module, are so valuable in practice.
Worked Example

A team attempting to fine-tune an extremely large model discovers it does not fit on their largest available single GPU, even after applying quantization and gradient checkpointing from earlier modules.

Splitting the model layers across two GPUs using model parallelism lets each device hold only half the model, finally allowing the fine-tuning run to proceed, at the cost of the inter-device communication and idle time tradeoffs covered in this topic, tradeoffs the team judges well worth accepting given the alternative was not being able to train the model at all.
Common Mistakes

items: Reaching for model parallelism when the model actually fits on a single device and data parallelism alone would have sufficed
Not accounting for the communication overhead introduced when data has to transfer between devices holding different model portions
Ignoring the device idle time risk inherent in a naive layer split without considering pipeline parallelism as an improvement
Assuming model parallelism and data parallelism are mutually exclusive, when they are often combined together in practice

blocks.text: Practice

For a model you have in mind, first check whether it would fit on a single device after quantization, and only if it genuinely would not, sketch how you might split its layers across two devices, noting where the communication handoff would need to happen.
Key Takeaway

Model parallelism splits the model itself across multiple devices, solving the specific problem of a model too large for any single device to hold, a fundamentally different problem from what data parallelism addresses, and it often gets combined with data parallelism in large scale training setups, though its added communication overhead and device utilization complexity mean it is best reserved for cases where a model genuinely does not fit otherwise.
